name: TLS and HTTPS
intent: Protect traffic between a client and a server so that nobody on the path can read it or change it, and so the client knows it is talking to the real server.
scenario: A customer logs in to a shop from café Wi-Fi. Anyone on that network can see every byte that crosses it, and a hostile network could even try to pose as the shop.
problem: Networks are not trustworthy. Without protection, the passwords and cards a user sends can be read by eavesdroppers, altered on the way, or sent to an impostor server. Encryption alone is not enough: the client must also be sure whose keys it is using.

howItWorks.title: The client says hello and the server shows a certificate
howItWorks.text: The client starts a TLS handshake by listing the protocol versions and cipher suites it supports. The server picks one and sends its certificate: a document that binds the server's public key to its domain name, signed by a certificate authority (CA).

howItWorks.title: The client verifies the certificate
howItWorks.text: The browser checks that the certificate is signed by a CA it trusts (directly or through a chain), has not expired or been revoked, and names the exact domain it is connecting to. If any check fails it shows a warning instead of proceeding, because that is how an impostor would look.

howItWorks.title: Both sides agree on a secret key without sending it
howItWorks.text: Using a key exchange (an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange in modern TLS), the two sides derive the same shared secret, while an eavesdropper who sees the whole exchange cannot. Because the keys are ephemeral, recorded traffic cannot be decrypted later even if the server's key is stolen (forward secrecy).

howItWorks.title: Traffic is encrypted and authenticated
howItWorks.text: From then on, a fast symmetric cipher (such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) encrypts every record and adds an authentication tag. An attacker sees only ciphertext, and any change to it is detected and the connection is dropped.

howItWorks.title: Operate it well
howItWorks.text: Get certificates from an automated CA (Let's Encrypt and similar), renew them before they expire, redirect HTTP to HTTPS and send HSTS so browsers never try plain HTTP again, and keep only modern protocol versions (TLS 1.2 and 1.3) enabled.

pros: Confidentiality: eavesdroppers see only encrypted data
Authenticity: the client knows it reached the real domain
Standard, widely supported and now nearly free
cons: The handshake adds a round trip or two (reduced in TLS 1.3 and with session resumption)
Certificates must be issued, deployed and renewed, and an expired one takes the site down
Terminating TLS at a load balancer means traffic inside may be unencrypted unless re-encrypted
Protects the connection only, not data once it is stored or processed
whenToUse: Every website and API, including internal service-to-service traffic (mutual TLS)
Anything carrying credentials, personal data, cookies or tokens
whenNotToUse: As your only protection: it does not stop attacks on the application itself, or protect data at rest
Skipping certificate checks in client code just to make an error go away
pitfalls: Letting certificates expire, which breaks every client at once
Disabling certificate validation in code or telling users to click through warnings
Serving a mix of HTTPS pages with HTTP resources
Offering old protocol versions and weak ciphers for compatibility

roles.label: Browser
roles.description: Verifies the certificate and encrypts requests.

roles.label: Server
roles.description: Proves its identity with a certificate and holds the private key.

roles.label: Certificate authority
roles.description: A trusted party that signs certificates.

quiz.question: A user joins a café network. An attacker runs a fake hotspot that presents a self-made certificate for shop.com. The connection is encrypted with a key exchange. What stops the user's browser from talking to the attacker?
options: Encryption alone, because the attacker cannot read the traffic
The key exchange, because only the real server can finish it
The HTTP to HTTPS redirect on the shop's real site
Certificate validation against trusted CAs and the domain name
quiz.explanation: Encryption protects the channel but not the identity of the other end: the attacker can run a key exchange too. The client must verify that a trusted CA signed a certificate naming the exact domain, and it warns when that fails.

quiz.question: At 02:00 on a Sunday every client suddenly shows certificate errors, though the server is healthy. The certificate expired. What is the best lasting fix?
options: Automate issuance and renewal, and alert on days to expiry
Buy the longest-lived certificate available and set a calendar reminder
Tell clients to skip certificate validation until it is renewed
Redirect users to plain HTTP until the renewal is done
quiz.explanation: Certificates expire by design, so renewal has to be automatic and watched. A longer life with a manual reminder only delays the same failure. Skipping validation or dropping to HTTP removes the protection TLS provides.

quiz.question: A team's server uses TLS 1.3 with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman. Someone records a year of encrypted traffic, then steals the server's private key. Can the recorded sessions be decrypted?
options: Yes, because the private key decrypts the session keys sent in the handshake
Yes, unless the certificate is revoked after the theft
No, because the session keys came from ephemeral values never stored
No, because the certificate had already expired before the theft
quiz.explanation: With an ephemeral exchange the private key only signs the handshake and never protects the session keys, so recorded traffic stays safe (forward secrecy). Revocation and expiry do not change what was already recorded.
